evidence.quote: Most frameworks for teams of large language model (LLM) agents fix the team's shape inside the software: who talks to whom, how much is passed along, and what a human can do once a run has started. Human-team research has long asked those questions: where team phenomena live (in members or in their interaction), how team-level properties arise, and what separates what a team does from how a team is. I propose using that theory as the organizing lens for configuring, observing and intervening in LLM-agent teams, without assuming its findings transfer. I introduce teamknitt, a framework and open reference implementation in which a user configures a team of 1-16 AI agents for task completion, solution generation, achieving a goal or a research mission; selects one of fourteen deterministic routing topologies or a custom directed graph; chooses a sharing profile that limits what may travel along permitted routes; and binds sources, representations, work dependencies, handoffs and an expertise directory. The recorded process can be observed through non-system views (member reports and behavior) and system views (distributed problem-solving, differentiated transactive memory, interactive coordination, team dynamics). Interventions are explicit and human-led: reviewed reconfiguration between runs, planned disturbances, and private feedback, pause, resume or stop applied at dependency-wave boundaries, with "queued", "applied", "assembled", "understood" and "improved" kept as separate claims. Emergent states such as trust and shared understanding are declared unmeasured. This is an idea and system-description paper with falsifiable hypotheses on topology, information flow and intervention timing, including whether the fractal scaling of communication output between members, and between members on different models, relates to task and team performance. No comparative result is reported.

The present paper takes these distinctions seriously as design questions for LLM-agent
teams , while refusing the shortcut of assuming that human findings carry over. If the
organization of an agent team changes what it produces, a user should be able to choose the
organization explicitly, observe the work through more than one explanatory lens, and intervene
in ways whose scope is recorded. teamknitt is a concrete attempt to make that possible. It is a
follow-up to Labtune [ 32 ] , which treated laboratory organization and
information sharing as controlled variables for LLM-agent research, and to the author’s thesis
work on the dynamics of distributed software teams’ creative processes [ 31 ] .
Where Labtune offered six editable laboratory designs for research missions, teamknitt generalizes
the mission to tasks, brainstorming and goals, replaces lab designs with fourteen routing
topologies over 1–16 members, binds the team’s problem-solving structure explicitly, and adds
research-informed views and human-led intervention. It ships its own runtime and makes no
automated organizational improvement.

evidence.quote: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed as multi-agent systems rather than as a standalone model operating within a single context. Recent agent harnesses allow the model to instantiate worker agents and to author the executable workflow that coordinates them, shifting the design of system structure from developers to the model at run time. The quality of this organization therefore constitutes a distinct capability, yet existing benchmarks either measure end-to-end task completion or evaluate coordination under structures specified in advance. We formalize this capability as workflow orchestration and introduce WorkflowArena, a benchmark of 145 long-horizon tasks spanning 8 professional domains, from software engineering and formal mathematics to legal analysis and 3D production. Each task specifies an initial workspace and an integrated deliverable composed of interdependent components, which is assessed by a hidden verifier. Agents determine autonomously whether and how to delegate, and all delegation is recorded, enabling joint evaluation of deliverable quality and the organization of the underlying work. Experiments with nine models show that no single configuration performs best across all domains and that systems exhibit distinct delegation strategies: at high effort, Claude models in Claude Code invoke workflows less frequently but with larger worker groups, whereas GPT models in Codex delegate more frequently in smaller units. When the executing model is held fixed on a challenging subset of tasks, workflows authored by Claude Opus 5.5 substantially improve weaker executors, indicating that workflow organization is itself a measurable determinant of task performance.

ReAct and Reflexion interleave execution with observation and feedback, ReWOO separates planning from tool observations, and LLMCompiler schedules function calls in parallel [ 1 , 2 , 40 , 9 ] . FlowBench studies planning with supplied workflow knowledge, WorFBench evaluates generated sequence and graph structures together with their downstream utility, and OrchBench isolates orchestration-plan quality through deterministic simulation and validates its scores against real executions [ 18 , 19 , 20 ] . SkillsBench evaluates procedural knowledge by comparing matched conditions with and without skills [ 41 ] . These studies separate the quality of a workflow structure from its realized utility, but they evaluate structures largely offline or in simulation. Interface design and simple execution pipelines can also materially affect task performance, as SWE-agent and Agentless illustrate [ 3 , 42 ] , which motivates evaluating the model together with its harness. WorkflowArena evaluates workflows as they execute on professional artifacts, where the model revises its plan from the results its workers return and the time spent on orchestration counts against the task.

We evaluate complete model–harness configurations under a common end-to-end wall-clock budget of four hours. Each task starts from a clean container workspace, and the budget is shared by the main agent and its workers. It covers all activity after the task starts, whereas environment preparation and grading lie outside it. Because the budget is shared, organization has a cost: parallel workers can shorten the critical path, but every step needed to coordinate them consumes the same time as the work itself. Task outcomes therefore reflect deliverable quality under a fixed time constraint, while token consumption and estimated inference cost characterize the resources each configuration uses.

The agent has full access to the task workspace, including the shell, tests, and direct file editing. It is also given a Workflow tool that launches background workflows with up to 16 concurrent workers and allows the agent to inspect, stop, and revise them. We write Workflow for this tool and its invocations, and workflow for the general concept. Each worker is a fresh instance of the agent itself, with the same model, harness, and effort. Because workers start from a fresh context and share only the workspace, the agent must decide what each worker needs to know, which makes context allocation part of the evaluated behavior. Native sub-agent mechanisms are disabled, so every delegation passes through the Workflow tool and is recorded. Using the tool remains optional, which leaves the decision to delegate entirely to the agent. The agent may revise its workflow in response to public execution feedback until it stops or exhausts the budget, after which the verifier scores the final artifact. Each execution thus yields a trace of Workflow invocations, worker executions, and revisions, together with the time and tokens consumed by the main agent and each worker.

evidence.quote: Test-time scaling improves the performance of a fixed model by spending more computation at inference. There are two common ways to spend it on agents when a verifier can score every attempt. Best-of-N sampling runs many independent agents and keeps the best result but saturates quickly. One large team of collaborating agents can score higher but stops improving as it grows. Can we get the best of both? Our method, parallel agent teams, does so by sampling many small teams in parallel and keeping the best team's result. We test it on 12 long-horizon tasks from GPU kernels and formal proofs to exploit development. With a 27B model and a budget of 100 agents, parallel teams of ten beat parallel agents on 10 of 12 tasks and beat one team of 100 on all four tasks where we ran such large teams. At equal dollar cost the same parallel teams beat a frontier model on half the tasks. A simple statistical model shows that individual agents lose because their many samples have a low mean and that one large team loses because a single sample gets no gain from variance. Sampling many small teams in parallel balances a high mean with the gain from variance. Parallel agent teams thus offer a more effective way to scale test-time compute.

Test-time compute lets a fixed pre-trained model do better by spending more computation at inference ( Snell et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) . An ideal method would turn more compute into better results steadily. We study tasks where a verifier can score every attempt and only the best solution matters. Many tasks for coding agents have this form ( Chan et al., 2025 ; Wijk et al., 2025 ) because a scorer can check each attempt automatically and only the fastest kernel or the finished proof matters. On such tasks there are two common ways to spend more compute on agents. The first is best-of- N N sampling, one of the strongest methods when a verifier is available ( Chen et al., 2021 ; Cobbe et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2022 ; Brown et al., 2024 ) . It runs N N independent agents and keeps the one with the highest score. Yet best-of- N N over individual agents saturates quickly. In our experiments, 50 agents already reach 81% to 100% of the gain that 100 agents reach.

Parallel agent teams combine the two by applying best-of- N N to independent teams (Figure 1 a), so a sample is one team. We measure compute as a budget of B B agents that each run for the same fixed time. It buys N = B / k N=B/k teams of size k k . Parallel agents ( k = 1 k=1 ) and one big team ( k = B k=B ) are the two ends of this family, and parallel teams lie in between. We use teams of ten unless stated otherwise and study the team size in Section 3.1 .

evidence.quote: Building agentic pipelines that achieve high task performance while keeping cost and latency low requires jointly optimizing heterogeneous and coupled design choices, including prompts, topology, model selection, and tool policies. Manually searching this combinatorial design space is expensive and time-consuming, while existing automated optimizers typically operate within a predefined subset of this space, modify the pipeline monolithically, or provide little structured evidence for pipeline changes. To mitigate these challenges, we introduce the Decomposed Credit-Assignment Framework (DeCAF), which adapts the design space to the given benchmark and pipeline, optimizes each dimension separately, and generates reasoning traces for every decision. Given a task specification, benchmark examples, and a seed pipeline, DeCAF identifies relevant optimization dimensions and generates diverse experimental hypotheses for each. Independent coding-agent sessions then optimize each dimension under a restricted edit scope, jointly evaluating performance, inference cost, and latency while recording all hypotheses, edits, and outcomes of each experiment. A final synthesis session combines compatible findings across all dimensions and uses a component-level trajectory evaluator, which derives role-specific rubrics from each agent's instructions, to localize underperforming components and guide cross-dimension revisions. Across a diverse suite of agentic benchmarks, DeCAF improves average task performance by 2.58 percentage points, while reducing inference cost by 4.30% and end-to-end latency by 42.45% compared to the best overall baseline.

Let P 0 = ( G , Θ ) P_{0}=(G,\Theta) denote a seed agentic pipeline, where G = ( V , E ) G=(V,E) is its computational graph and Θ \Theta contains configurable choices such as prompts, model assignments, inference parameters, context policies, tools, and control flow. Executing a pipeline P P on input x x produces an output y ^ \hat{y} and a trajectory τ \tau containing intermediate node inputs, outputs, tool calls, and system state. For a development set 𝒟 dev = { x i } i = 1 N \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{dev}}=\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} , we associate each pipeline with the objective vector

where q q , c c , and ℓ \ell measure task performance, inference cost, and end-to-end latency, respectively. A candidate dominates another if it achieves no lower task performance, no greater cost or latency, and strictly improves at least one objective. While objectives can be folded into a single scalar by weighted combination, e.g., 0.8 × q ⁡ ( P , x i ) − 0.1 × c ⁡ ( P , x i ) − 0.1 × ℓ ⁡ ( P , x i ) 0.8\times q(P,x_{i})-0.1\times c(P,x_{i})-0.1\times\ell(P,x_{i}) , this scalarization commits to weights before the attainable trade-offs are known, yields one operating point per run, and has well-known failure modes (e.g., non-convex regions of the frontier are unreachable by any linear weighting) ( Deb et al., 2002 ) . Therefore, rather than collapsing these objectives into a fixed weighted scalar, DeCAF maintains non-dominated candidates, preserving operating points with different deployment trade-offs. The held-out test set is not exposed during any part of DeCAF .

For every dimension D k D_{k} , DeCAF creates a copy of the seed pipeline and launches a fresh coding-agent session for optimization. The session receives the task specification, development data, dimension definition, and hypotheses ℋ k \mathcal{H}_{k} . It has a primary editable scope ℳ k \mathcal{M}_{k} and is instructed to focus its search on dimension D k D_{k} . However, supporting changes are allowed. For example, when modifying topology, new prompts need to be written for the agents. The ‘topology’ still remains the primary optimization dimension, while ‘prompt’ becomes the secondary or supportive dimension. The coding agent iteratively selects or adapts a hypothesis, implements the corresponding changes, and evaluates the candidate. Each dimension maintains a non-dominated archive

where ND \operatorname{ND} removes candidates dominated by another member of the archive. A candidate need not strictly dominate the seed to be retained. For example, a performance gain at a modest cost increase may represent a useful operating point on the observed frontier. Every attempted experiment is also recorded in a FINDINGS.md artifact. The record includes the motivating hypothesis, affected components, implemented change, measured objectives, whether the candidate was retained, observed regressions, and conclusions for later optimization. Failed experiments are preserved so that the final optimizer can avoid repeating ineffective changes and can reason about benchmark-specific trade-offs. Because all dimension-level sessions begin from the same seed and vary only their assigned design dimension, their outcomes provide controlled, conditional evidence about which classes of interventions are effective around P 0 P_{0} . To reduce the wall-clock optimization time, the sessions run in parallel. Each dimension returns its archive and findings, ( 𝒜 k , ℱ k ) (\mathcal{A}_{k},\mathcal{F}_{k}) , to the final stage.

The synthesis agent uses these diagnostics together with the successful and unsuccessful findings from the dimension-level searches. It tests combinations of promising changes and re-evaluates every composed pipeline end-to-end on D dev D_{\mathrm{dev}} . When a combination regresses, node_eval can help identify where the interaction failed and guide a targeted repair, such as changing a prompt or adjusting the information passed between stages. Importantly, node_eval is only a diagnostic tool: pipeline changes are still accepted or rejected using the task-performance, cost, and latency objectives. The synthesis stage maintains a final non-dominated archive using the same update rule as Eq. 2 . A final pipeline and harness is selected via the optimizer LLM from this archive using development-set evidence and is then evaluated on the held-out test set.

Seed pipelines and Models. Each optimization begins from a fixed seed pipeline. For AppWorld, we use a single ReAct coding harness, backed by Claude-Sonnet-4.6 at medium effort, with other Claude models as choices for optimization. For LiveCodeBench, we use a sequential generator–critic–refiner pipeline in which all three nodes are initialized with GPT-5.4-nano, and GPT-5.4 family of models given for optimization. For AgentDojo, we use the seed harness with a single-stage ReAct agent using Qwen-3.5-397b-a17b-FP8 model, and Gemma ( Team et al., 2026 ) and Qwen ( Team, 2026 ) family of models are available as optimization choices. For PostTrainBench, a single Claude Code post-training agent backed by Claude-Sonnet-5 at high effort is used as the seed. Opus and Haiku variants are given as choices for optimization. DeCAF uses Claude Code as the coding agent and uses /goal mechanism 1 1 1 https://code.claude.com/docs/en/goal to maintain the optimization objective. Every optimizer is run twice and the final table reports the average and standard error across both runs.

Table 1 reports the one-time cost and wall-clock time required to run each optimizer. Since DeCAF decomposes the search space into independent dimensions, coding agents for each dimension can run in parallel. This reduces the wall-clock time of DeCAF significantly compared to Meta-Harness, where experiments run sequentially. The only exception being PostTrainBench, where we ran each dimension sequentially due to the bottleneck on the GPU resources. This makes DeCAF 27.6 % 27.6\% faster on average ( 37.65 % 37.65\% faster if we remove PostTrainBench). However, this decomposition and better exploration comes at a cost, it increases the total cost of optimization. On average, DeCAF is 17.98 % 17.98\% more expensive than Meta-Harness. There are two major contributions of this increased cost. First, the optimizer is forced to explore performance using the stronger (and generally more expensive) models. This increases the cost of evaluation of the pipeline on the validation set. Second, the node_eval tool makes up roughly 6 % 6\% of the optimization cost of DeCAF . This tool takes in multiple trajectories of the agent which increases the input token cost. Due to the heavy cost of this tool, it is only given to the final synthesizer coding agent, not the dimension-level coding agents.

evidence.quote: Low-bit quantization reduces the inference cost of LLM agents but can compromise task success. Examining failed rollouts, we find that quantized agents overlook task requirements or environmental conditions, producing environment transitions that diverge from successful full-precision references. Correcting these behavioral divergences remains difficult: offline data may miss the student's failure contexts, while its own rollouts may provide few correct responses in those contexts. We introduce SteerDistill, a quantization-aware distillation method in which a full-precision teacher guides the student to revise failed responses and iteratively refines its guidance using feedback from student execution. This closed-loop teacher steering produces locally verified behavioral corrections. We internalize these corrections by training the student without guidance to match the steered student's predictions at corrected turns and the full-precision teacher's at other turns, enabling unassisted inference. Across five agentic benchmarks and three models, SteerDistill exceeds the strongest quantized baseline by 1.67--2.18 points in average score under W4A16 and stays within one point of BF16. On $τ^2$-Bench, it outperforms QeRL by 1.84 percentage points in success rate using 67% fewer training GPU hours and produces shorter successful trajectories than the quantized baselines.

evidence.quote: Web-facing AI agents repeatedly access webpages, documents, repositories, and tool responses, yet reading interfaces often expose entire objects when only sparse evidence is needed. This over-reading increases token and latency costs and can dilute relevant evidence. We present SparseRead, a reusable reading control layer that governs content admission without modifying the agent model. Its Read Intent Protocol tracks evolving needs and source coverage; Adaptive Reader Backends select how evidence is located and exposed; and the Budgeted Read Gate bounds cumulative raw exposure per episode with faithful full-view fallback. A unified Reader interface supports interchangeable evidence acquisition across heterogeneous resources. Across six models, including Claude Opus 5, and five scenarios, SparseRead reduces total tokens by up to 92.9% and wall time by up to 89.0%, preserving or improving task quality in 97% settings. On Web deep-search tasks, it reduces tokens by 31.0--43.0% and task completion time by 23.0--37.0%. Ablations validate the three designs, while integration with three agent frameworks demonstrates portability.

Read outcomes can further inform cost estimates: repeated access or escalation indicates extra reading work, whereas a verification request is not itself a failure. Such behavioral signals do not establish evidence correctness. Likewise, source anchors and fingerprints establish provenance, not relevance or sufficiency. This division keeps reliability calibration separate from cost adaptation. Specialized Readers and new evidence methods continue to use the same interface.

Evidence success. Each calibration request specifies required support or an expected source-operation result. Evidence acquisition succeeds when the returned content supplies that support within the requested scope and retains valid provenance; an exact operation succeeds when its output matches the specified result for that scope. These binary request-level outcomes inform p ^ valid \widehat{p}_{\mathrm{valid}} . For each configuration and group, p ^ valid \widehat{p}_{\mathrm{valid}} is the lower end of a 95% Wilson interval over these outcomes, and the threshold is τ = 0.6 \tau=0.6 , fixed before evaluation. A group with fewer than 20 calibration requests is not adaptive: it uses the default configuration for its artifact type, and falls back to a full view if that configuration does not meet the threshold. Cost profiles account for evidence exposure and further Reader work, while evaluation reports total tokens and wall time separately. The estimate C ^ \widehat{C} is measured in characters: exposed characters, a fixed per-call overhead for Reader execution, and the mean follow-up exposure observed for the group during calibration. Reliability is calibrated once; evaluation updates only cost estimates.

evidence.quote: Visual interaction models that support users during ongoing physical tasks require evaluation in closed loop, where assistant responses can change subsequent user behavior and task outcomes. Existing benchmarks largely rely on offline replay and therefore cannot capture these effects. We introduce Interactive Visual Gym, a framework for closed-loop evaluation and training of visual interaction models through joint simulation of executable task environments and human users. We contribute three simulators that recreate everyday tasks and human-aligned action spaces across cooking, household manipulation, and mobile-interface domains, together with a persona-conditioned user simulation harness that collaborates with the assistant while incorporating controlled execution errors and other out-of-plan behaviors. We instantiate the framework as IVG-Bench, a benchmark with 315 interaction scenarios. Evaluating state-of-the-art VLMs as visual interaction models reveals substantial limitations: the best-performing model, Gemini 4 Argon, completes only 53.4% of tasks within the time limit, exhibits significant weaknesses in factual grounding and actionable guidance, and is often too slow to prevent errors when response latency is considered. We verify our evaluation protocol with a human study which finds 78.5% agreement between our interaction-quality metric and participant preferences. We further show that the environments provide useful learning signals: in a proof-of-concept GRPO experiment, closed-loop training improves both task success and interaction quality for Qwen3.5-4B model in our cooking environment.

evidence.quote: Agentic workloads are a major source of LLM inference demand. Existing prefill--decode (PD) disaggregated serving systems offer limited flexibility for runtime adaptation of compute allocation and KV cache management, and rely on coarse signals that only partly capture the diverse and dynamic agent workload. These limitations lead to load imbalance between prefill and decode nodes and eviction of KV caches that agents will reuse. We present Evolving Infra, an agent-adaptive serving framework that adapts compute allocation to agent workloads and KV cache management to agent context management at runtime. We decouple compute allocation from key--value (KV) cache management, allowing nodes to switch efficiently between prefill and decode. Building on this design, an online planner matches the PD split to workload composition, while an agent-aware distributed KV manager guides cache eviction and transfer with signals from agent context management. Across coding, math, and computer-use tasks with GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6 on up to 256 GB300 GPUs, Evolving Infra reduces mean end-to-end request latency and P95 TTFT by up to 4.1x and 14x over Dynamo, NVIDIA's production framework.

evidence.quote: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) suggests that neural networks are converging toward similar representation spaces. As language models become more capable, their representations are aligning with those of vision models. However, recent work has questioned whether this trend continues to hold for newer language models. Moreover, it has been shown that representation similarity metrics can be confounded by model depth and width, requiring appropriate baselines for interpretation. In this work, we first investigate where alignment emerges between unimodal models across model layers and representation dimensions. Next, we find that the PRH capability-alignment trend persists for newer models as long as the captions are sufficiently clean and informative. Finally, we contextualize cross-modal alignment, introducing unimodal and multimodal baselines on various datasets. Our results show that the cross-modal representational alignment of unimodal models can surpass that of explicitly aligned vision-language models, but remains substantially behind the alignment observed for models of the same modality. Code is available at https://github.com/ExplainableML/prh-closer-look.

evidence.quote: We present FAME-QP, a GPU-accelerated solver for dense quadratic programs arising in linear model predictive control. FAME-QP combines constraint-dependent operator representations with fused single- and two-kernel iterations replayed through CUDA graphs, automatically selecting the execution configuration through device calibration and problem-specific timing. It probes a cached operator bank to select the initial penalty and updates operators lazily when problem matrices change. Numerical benchmarks and simulated humanoid and quadrotor control experiments demonstrate reduced latency relative to competing GPU solvers while maintaining solution accuracy and control performance.

evidence.quote: Local decoding usually fixes one weight precision for the whole generation. We study a different allocation: store 8-bit weights, decode with their top 4 bits, and redo a step at 8 bits only when the low-precision output distribution looks uncertain (entropy above a threshold or a small top-two margin). Quantization is simulated, the model is Qwen3-0.6B, and the benchmark is GSM8K. Cost is counted in weight bytes read per token. On 36724 replayed steps the entropy of the low pass ranks argmax flips with AUC 0.93. At a 15% escalation budget it catches 78% of flips and the margin gate 94%, against the 15% expected for a random gate of equal rate (a computed expectation, not a run). In 150 live problems all-high scores 64.0% and all-low 55.3% (McNemar p=0.053). An entropy gate with a 16% escalation rate scores 62.7% at 0.87 of the all-high weight bytes. Its paired difference is -1.3 (-8.0 to +5.3) points to all-high and +7.3 (+0.0 to +14.7) points to all-low (p=0.080), so the live data do not separate the gate from either end. Verified speculation reaches zero KL at similar bytes in the same cost model. A live random control, a thinking-mode phase rule, a second model and live KL were not run.

evidence.quote: Large language model (LLM) shopping assistants now recommend products in multi-turn conversations. However, reliable evaluation faces Data scarcity and Difficulty Standardizing Criteria. To address these obstacles, we introduce CARTBench for CART (Complex and Ambiguous Requests with Timelines). For Data scarcity, we curate cases from real commercial shopping needs across 17 retail domains, pairing timestamped dialogue with 1,603 product records. For Difficulty Standardizing Criteria, we develop case-specific rubrics guided by Ideal Response Principles, distilled from excellent replies manually selected from successfully completed orders. These principles also guide Principle-Guided CART Prompting, our structured recommendation strategy. The experimental benchmark contains 1,328 expert-annotated criteria across Core, Excellence, and Safety. To answer the CART question, we evaluate 7 flagship commercial API models, including GPT-6.1-Sol and Claude-Opus-5, and 35B+ parameters open-weight models. In the first full-suite evaluation under the frozen rubrics, 3 of 10 models exceed 90% on Core, while none exceeds 45% on Excellence. Therefore, we identify an understanding-to-execution gap between required behavior and high-quality purchase advice. To examine these limitations, we diagnose shared failures in product evidence and unresolved needs, linked to changing requirements and decisive unknowns. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Da1yuqin/CARTBench.

evidence.quote: Weight-space programming allows language models to read a trained neural network's weights and edit them. This opens the door to ``training'' by reasoning rather than through gradient descent. Prior work has demonstrated its functionality and promise for game-playing networks and fixing specific failures in language models, even extending to diffusion models. In this work, we present its applicability to models trained on biosignal data, specifically EEG and ECG data. We show that frontier models are not only able to debug specific faults planted in biosignal-based models without being told what these faults are, but are even capable of writing all the weights of a network from scratch, given only the architecture, the task, and a minimal set of training subjects. In particular, in one set of experiments, a language model was able to match standard gradient-descent training using $6\times$ fewer training subjects, through reasoning alone and without any gradient descent step. Networks written by Claude Opus 5.5 also scored higher than classic hand-crafted EEG pipelines (alpha band power, and common spatial patterns with linear discriminant analysis) when built from the same 5 subjects. We also highlight some of the limitations, which include the inability of language models to improve already well-trained classification models, and their incapacity to reliably recognize, from the weights alone, the task a network was trained on. Overall, our results indicate that weight-space programming can be useful for small networks, such as those deployed on edge devices and wearables, but the concept still requires further investigation before it can be used in practice.

evidence.quote: Different optimizers impose different geometries on parameter updates. Adaptive methods such as Adam and AdamW use coordinate-wise updates, while matrix-aware optimizers such as Muon utilize weight-matrix structure through orthogonalized updates. For Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), however, the effective geometry of its weight matrices is shaped not only by its learned channel-mixing weights, but also by the graph-propagated representations it acts on. Thus, even if an update is well normalized as a matrix, its effect on the layer output can be amplified when applied to graph-propagated features. To address this gap, we introduce GraphMuon, a graph-aware optimizer that adapts Muon's matrix updates to the covariance structure of graph-propagated layer inputs. GraphMuon performs orthogonalization in a metric defined by these propagated representations and normalizes step sizes according to the update's induced effect on the layer representation. We show that theoretically, vanilla Muon can suffer from graph-induced update amplification, while our GraphMuon can mitigate this effect. As such, our GraphMuon yields a graph-metric analogue of Muon's polar update step. Empirically, GraphMuon achieves $1.32\times$-$2.42\times$ validation-loss time-to-target speedups over AdamW on three large-scale OGB benchmarks. Across 15 dataset-architecture configurations spanning node classification, inductive graph classification, and graph regression, it achieves lower time-to-target in 13 cases, while maintaining competitive or superior predictive performance. Code is available at https://github.com/guy-hadad/GraphMuon.

evidence.quote: AI agents deployed on the open web are becoming more capable of performing actions that may breach contractual provisions and violate computer security laws. In this paper, we introduce ScrapeBench, the first agentic benchmark for empirically evaluating the legal compliance of AI agents with website scraping policies, namely terms of service (ToS) and $\texttt{robots.txt}$ directives. Across widely used closed-weight and open-weight AI agents, we find that most agents exhibit low compliance rates (< 5%) when instructed to scrape websites in our sample of 1,626 popular websites that explicitly prohibit scraping. In addition, we observe that even where AI agents actively check the applicable ToS and $\texttt{robots.txt}$, they continue to exhibit low compliance rates. Conversely, in our sample of 269 websites that do not prohibit scraping, we observe that agents sometimes refuse to scrape despite it being lawful, such as Claude Opus 4.6 exhibiting an over-refusal rate of 98.5%. Our human baseline experiments (n = 180 participants) suggest that humans exhibit compliance rates comparable to AI agents but over-refuse at much higher rates.

We conduct experiments with eight different legal priming prompts (detailed in Table 3 ) that aim to investigate changes in the legal compliance of AI agents under pressure and other conditions. As a baseline, we start with a simple neutral prompt (P1) of “ Scrape the landing page of { domain }”. Legal priming is then induced by gradually increasing the pressure in natural language in each prompt. This includes adding implicit and explicit instructions to comply with the ToS and robots.txt (P2, P3), linking URLs and pasting the text content of a website’s ToS and robots.txt (P4, P5, P6), and combining all these together (P7). 6 6 6 In appending the ToS text, we set a limit of 100,000 characters and truncate the remaining. We observe that most websites’ ToS do not reach this limit. Likewise, if a website does not have a ToS or robots.txt file, a placeholder string “ This website does not have terms of service / robots.txt. ” is substituted. Separately, an adversarial prompt (P8) tests agents’ responses to an instruction to ignore the website’s ToS and robots.txt .

evidence.quote: Local language models can save memory by storing weights in fewer bits, and they can reduce sensitivity to the order of answer options by averaging a few reorderings. We ask whether the first makes the second worse, and which is the cheaper way to spend a fixed budget. On Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B with simulated round-to-nearest weight quantization (8, 6, 4 and 3 bits, fp16 reference), read from the logits of the letters A to D on ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, MMLU and HellaSwag (300 items each), 6 bits lose no accuracy against fp16 (they score +1.8 (+1.0 to +2.5) and +0.9 (+0.3 to +1.5) points higher, which we do not explain), and 8 bits change it by -0.7 (-1.1 to -0.3) and -0.4 (-0.7 to -0.2) points. At 4 bits the answer-slot skew rises from 0.15 to 0.53 (0.6B) and from 0.07 to 0.12 (1.7B); Gaussian noise at the same weight SNR gives 0.15 and 0.37 (two draws) and 0.19 (one draw), so the control is inconclusive on whether rounding adds slot skew beyond equal-power noise. Flip rates rise but stay below an accuracy-matched baseline of independent uniform errors. Averaging four cyclic orders recovers +12.6 points at 4 bits for 0.6B (+5.3 at fp16). We price bits and passes in one machine-independent unit, weight bytes read times passes. In cost-matched pairs, extra orders beat extra bits only when the weights have 6 or more bits, and the decision table reduces to: use 6-bit weights and spend the rest of the budget on up to four orders, one pass each. Everything is simulated on two small models with the simplest quantizer; a title-level search found no earlier study of quantization together with option order.

evidence.quote: Typed-decision encoders answer a question about a text in one forward pass, but their behaviour outside English is rarely measured on a fixed yardstick. We release PolyRoute: 322 native-language support messages in 12 languages and 9 writing systems, 156 code-mixed or romanised messages (Hinglish, Spanglish, Arabizi), 967 optional native training rows, and a protocol for a three-way department-routing decision. Labels come from Qwen3.8-27B with a blind second pass (91% of candidates kept); an independent model, gemma4-31b, agrees on 97.2% of test items, and the largest character 5-gram similarity between any test text and any training text is 0.33. A leaderboard of 13 systems gives 61.2% for the English-root checkpoint, 77.3% for the shipped multilingual one and 96.6% for the best fine-tune; TF-IDF with logistic regression reaches 91.9%. On four withheld languages the three multilingual systems score 77%, 90% and 93%. On code-mixed text the English root (85%) is nominally ahead of the shipped multilingual checkpoint (79%; p=0.134). The split resolves differences only above about 4 points. All texts and labels are LLM-generated.

evidence.quote: Which representation should be probed in a transformer-based foundation model? Recent work shows that the standard practice of probing the final layer is often suboptimal, as intermediate layers can provide better features. Yet, representations are still largely studied along depth alone, treating each transformer block as an atomic unit. In this work, we analyze transformer representations layer by layer, module by module. Through more than 144,000 linear probing evaluations of vision foundation models (VFMs) and large language models (LLMs), we show that layer and module choices should be considered jointly: the best layer-module pair yields substantially larger gains over the final-layer residual stream than the best layer with the residual stream fixed. Moreover, module performance can vary substantially across layers, showing that useful representations cannot be characterized by depth alone. Building on these findings, we evaluate simple fixed probing strategies: the final-layer feedforward activation (Act@100) for vision and the second normalization layer at 60% depth (LN2@60) for language. These strategies improve over the probing baseline in a majority of evaluations and recover, on average, 42% and 86% of the gains from probing the best layer-module pair for vision and language, respectively. For VFMs, these gains increase with the transfer difficulty between pretraining and downstream data.
